MSME.Description: Wholesale of machinery, equipment, and supplies
Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
2) Move inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items) and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up purchase orders, supplier/customer lists and billing data.
5) Test backup power (generator/UPS) and maintain an emergency fuel plan to keep essential equipment running.
Flood.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
5) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.
Flood.Reference.Sources: NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Floods — https://nidm.gov.in/pdf/guidelines/floods.pdf ; NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Urban Flooding — https://nidm.gov.in/pdf/guidelines/new/management_urban_flooding.pdf ; FEMA – P‑348 Protecting Building Utility Systems From Flood Damage — https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/fema_p-348_protecting_building_utility_systems_from_flood_damage_2017.pdf ; ISO – ISO 22301 Business continuity management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/75106.html
Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items): wrap palletized goods, raise critical stock, and cover machinery/equipment to prevent rainwater ingress.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.
Cyclone.Reference.Sources: NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Cyclones — https://nidm.gov.in/PDF/pubs/NDMA/4.pdf ; IMD – Cyclone Warning Services (overview) — https://mausam.imd.gov.in/imd_latest/contents/pdf/pubbrochures/Cyclone%20Warning%20Services.pdf ; BIS/Building Codes – Wind loads (IS 875 Part 3) reference — https://www.iitk.ac.in/nicee/IITK-GSDMA/W02.pdf ; ISO – ISO 22301 Business continuity management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/75106.html
Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
2) Install and clearly label emergency shutoffs for electricity, gas and compressed air; ensure staff know how to operate them.
3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up purchase orders, supplier/customer lists and billing data and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.
Earthquake.Reference.Sources: NDMA – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes — https://ndma.gov.in/sites/default/files/PDF/Guidelines/earthquakes.pdf ; NDMA – Simplified Guidelines for Earthquake Safety of Buildings — https://ndma.gov.in/sites/default/files/PDF/Guidelines/Simplified_Guidelines_for_earthquake.pdf ; BIS – Seismic design standards (e.g., IS 1893, IS 4326, IS 13920) — BIS Standards (refer latest editions) ; ISO – ISO 22301 Business continuity management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/75106.html
Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).
2) Before/after heavy rain, inspect and clear surface drains and culverts to prevent water buildup that can trigger slope failure.
3) Keep critical areas away from slope edges: avoid stacking heavy inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items) near retaining walls or steep embankments.
4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for access disruption: identify alternate routes/warehousing, and maintain contact lists for logistics, utilities and local authorities.
Landslide.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a geotechnical and slope-stability assessment; implement site-specific recommendations as a priority.
2) Improve slope drainage: lined drains, sub-surface drainage and proper runoff routing to reduce saturation of soil/rock.
3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

2) Improve slope drainage: lined drains, sub-surface drainage and proper runoff routing to reduce saturation of soil/rock.
3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

MSME.Description: Retail sale of food, beverages, and tobacco in specialized stores
Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
2) Move inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items) and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up purchase orders, supplier/customer lists and billing data.
5) Test backup power (generator/UPS) and maintain an emergency fuel plan to keep essential equipment running.
Flood.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
5) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.
6) Reconfigure storage: elevate high-value SKUs, use flood-resistant racking, and digitize inventory for faster claims and replenishment.

Drought.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize water for critical process and hygiene steps in the storefront/warehouse and loading areas; postpone non-critical cleaning/wash-downs where safe and permitted.
3) Introduce quick efficiency measures: low-flow nozzles, trigger hoses, dry-cleaning/sweeping before washing, and reuse of non-contact rinse water where appropriate.
4) Secure contingency supply: agreements for tanker/municipal supply and on-site storage; test water quality if used for food/health-related activities.
5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.

Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items): wrap palletized goods, raise critical stock, and cover machinery/equipment to prevent rainwater ingress.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.

Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
2) Install and clearly label emergency shutoffs for electricity, gas and compressed air; ensure staff know how to operate them.
3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up purchase orders, supplier/customer lists and billing data and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.

Heatwave.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Adopt a simple Heat Action Plan: monitor heat alerts, designate a supervisor, and define work-rest and hydration breaks.
2) Reduce heat exposure: shift heavy work to cooler hours, increase ventilation, provide shaded rest areas and cool drinking water.
3) Protect heat-sensitive inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items) and equipment: verify cooling setpoints, service HVAC/chillers, and keep critical spares for cooling systems.
4) Train staff to recognize heat illness and respond quickly; maintain a first-aid protocol and emergency contact arrangements.
5) Reduce indoor heat gain: close blinds during peak sun, use fans/air movement safely, and limit use of heat-generating equipment in peak hours.
Heatwave.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Improve building thermal performance: cool roofs (reflective coatings), insulation, shading and natural ventilation design.
2) Upgrade to energy-efficient cooling systems sized for peak heat; consider zoned cooling for critical areas to reduce costs.
3) Install temperature monitoring and alarms (cold rooms, server rooms, critical production spaces) with preventive maintenance schedules.
4) Create longer-term workforce adaptations: heat-safe uniforms/PPE, annual training before summer, and paid rest breaks during severe heat alerts.
5) Reduce dependency on grid power: solar + battery/backup solutions to keep essential cooling and IT running during peak demand outages.

Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).
2) Before/after heavy rain, inspect and clear surface drains and culverts to prevent water buildup that can trigger slope failure.
3) Keep critical areas away from slope edges: avoid stacking heavy inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items) near retaining walls or steep embankments.
4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for access disruption: identify alternate routes/warehousing, and maintain contact lists for logistics, utilities and local authorities.

3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.

Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.

3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up purchase orders, supplier/customer lists and billing data and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).

Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).
2) Before/after heavy rain, inspect and clear surface drains and culverts to prevent water buildup that can trigger slope failure.
3) Keep critical areas away from slope edges: avoid stacking heavy inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items) near retaining walls or steep embankments.
4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for access disruption: identify alternate routes/warehousing, and maintain contact lists for logistics, utilities and local authorities.
Landslide.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a geotechnical and slope-stability assessment; implement site-specific recommendations as a priority.
2) Improve slope drainage: lined drains, sub-surface drainage and proper runoff routing to reduce saturation of soil/rock.
3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

MSME.Description: Retail sale of cultural and recreation goods in specialized stores
Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
2) Move inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items) and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up purchase orders, supplier/customer lists and billing data.
5) Test backup power (generator/UPS) and maintain an emergency fuel plan to keep essential equipment running.

1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
5) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.
6) Reconfigure storage: elevate high-value SKUs, use flood-resistant racking, and digitize inventory for faster claims and replenishment.

MSME.Description: Retail trade not in stores, stalls, or markets
Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
2) Move inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items) and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up purchase orders, supplier/customer lists and billing data.
5) Test backup power (generator/UPS) and maintain an emergency fuel plan to keep essential equipment running.
Flood.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the storefront/warehouse and loading areas.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
5) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.

Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect inventory stock (high-value, perishable or fragile items): wrap palletized goods, raise critical stock, and cover machinery/equipment to prevent rainwater ingress.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.

Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:

4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for access disruption: identify alternate routes/warehousing, and maintain contact lists for logistics, utilities and local authorities.

1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the depots, parking yards and maintenance areas.

3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up route plans, driver rosters and dispatch/booking systems and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.

1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize water for critical process and hygiene steps in the depots, parking yards and maintenance areas; postpone non-critical cleaning/wash-downs where safe and permitted.

5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.

1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).

MSME.Description: Water transport
Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the depots, parking yards and maintenance areas.
2) Move cargo in transit and warehouse/depot stock and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up route plans, driver rosters and dispatch/booking systems.
5) Test backup power (generator/UPS) and maintain an emergency fuel plan to keep essential equipment running.
6) Pre-position fleet and cargo: move vehicles to higher ground, reroute deliveries, and inform customers of potential delays.
Flood.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the depots, parking yards and maintenance areas.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
5) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.

Drought.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize water for critical process and hygiene steps in the depots, parking yards and maintenance areas; postpone non-critical cleaning/wash-downs where safe and permitted.
3) Introduce quick efficiency measures: low-flow nozzles, trigger hoses, dry-cleaning/sweeping before washing, and reuse of non-contact rinse water where appropriate.
4) Secure contingency supply: agreements for tanker/municipal supply and on-site storage; test water quality if used for food/health-related activities.
5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.

Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect cargo and fleet: move vehicles to sheltered/high-ground parking, secure trailers/containers, and pre-plan alternative routes after landfall.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.
6) Develop a depot resilience plan: covered parking, wind-rated canopies, spare parts inventory, and rapid post-storm inspection protocols.

Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the depots, parking yards and maintenance areas.
2) Install and clearly label emergency shutoffs for electricity, gas and compressed air; ensure staff know how to operate them.
3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up route plans, driver rosters and dispatch/booking systems and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.

Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect cargo and fleet: move vehicles to sheltered/high-ground parking, secure trailers/containers, and pre-plan alternative routes after landfall.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.
6) Develop a depot resilience plan: covered parking, wind-rated canopies, spare parts inventory, and rapid post-storm inspection protocols.

Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the depots, parking yards and maintenance areas.
2) Install and clearly label emergency shutoffs for electricity, gas and compressed air; ensure staff know how to operate them.
3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up route plans, driver rosters and dispatch/booking systems and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.

Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).
2) Before/after heavy rain, inspect and clear surface drains and culverts to prevent water buildup that can trigger slope failure.
3) Keep critical areas away from slope edges: avoid stacking heavy cargo in transit and warehouse/depot stock near retaining walls or steep embankments.
4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for blocked roads: pre-map alternate routes, keep updated route advisories, and schedule deliveries with buffer time during monsoon.
Landslide.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a geotechnical and slope-stability assessment; implement site-specific recommendations as a priority.
2) Improve slope drainage: lined drains, sub-surface drainage and proper runoff routing to reduce saturation of soil/rock.
3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

MSME.Description: Accommodation
Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the kitchen, dining/service area and storage.
2) Move food and beverage stock (including chilled items) and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up supplier lists, menus/pricing and booking/payment data.
5) Maintain cold chain and food safety: test backup power for refrigeration, monitor temperatures, and quarantine/discard any stock exposed to floodwater.
6) Prepare a safe restart plan: deep-clean and disinfect production/service areas, verify water quality, and document checks before reopening.
Flood.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the kitchen, dining/service area and storage.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Set up contracted alternate cold storage/3PL arrangements and pre-approved transport to relocate chilled/frozen stock during alerts.
5) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
6) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.
7) Formalize a HACCP/FSMS-based incident and restart protocol (quarantine, disposal, sanitation verification, and traceability).

1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize potable water for food-contact hygiene/CIP in the kitchen, dining/service area and storage; if quality is uncertain, stop production/service until safe water is available.

4) Secure contingency supply: agreements for tanker/municipal supply and on-site storage; test water quality if used for food/health-related activities.
5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.

Drought.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize potable water for food-contact hygiene/CIP in the kitchen, dining/service area and storage; if quality is uncertain, stop production/service until safe water is available.
3) Introduce quick efficiency measures: low-flow nozzles, trigger hoses, dry-cleaning/sweeping before washing, and reuse of non-contact rinse water where appropriate.
4) Secure contingency supply: agreements for tanker/municipal supply and on-site storage; test water quality if used for food/health-related activities.
5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.

Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect food and beverage stock (including chilled items): wrap palletized goods, raise critical stock, and cover machinery/equipment to prevent rainwater ingress.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
6) Plan for cold chain continuity: prioritize generator loads for refrigeration and limit door openings during outages.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.

Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the kitchen, dining/service area and storage.
2) Install and clearly label emergency shutoffs for electricity, gas and compressed air; ensure staff know how to operate them.
3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up supplier lists, menus/pricing and booking/payment data and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.

Heatwave.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Adopt a simple Heat Action Plan: monitor heat alerts, designate a supervisor, and define work-rest and hydration breaks.
2) Reduce heat exposure: shift heavy work to cooler hours, increase ventilation, provide shaded rest areas and cool drinking water.
3) Protect chilled/frozen stock: maintain refrigeration performance, log temperatures, and use backup power/ice contingency to avoid spoilage.
4) Train staff to recognize heat illness and respond quickly; maintain a first-aid protocol and emergency contact arrangements.
5) Reduce indoor heat gain: close blinds during peak sun, use fans/air movement safely, and limit use of heat-generating equipment in peak hours.
Heatwave.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Improve building thermal performance: cool roofs (reflective coatings), insulation, shading and natural ventilation design.
2) Upgrade to energy-efficient cooling systems sized for peak heat; consider zoned cooling for critical areas to reduce costs.
3) Install temperature monitoring and alarms (cold rooms, server rooms, critical production spaces) with preventive maintenance schedules.
4) Create longer-term workforce adaptations: heat-safe uniforms/PPE, annual training before summer, and paid rest breaks during severe heat alerts.
5) Reduce dependency on grid power: solar + battery/backup solutions to keep essential cooling and IT running during peak demand outages.

Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).
2) Before/after heavy rain, inspect and clear surface drains and culverts to prevent water buildup that can trigger slope failure.
3) Keep critical areas away from slope edges: avoid stacking heavy food and beverage stock (including chilled items) near retaining walls or steep embankments.
4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for access disruption: identify alternate routes/warehousing, and maintain contact lists for logistics, utilities and local authorities.
Landslide.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a geotechnical and slope-stability assessment; implement site-specific recommendations as a priority.
2) Improve slope drainage: lined drains, sub-surface drainage and proper runoff routing to reduce saturation of soil/rock.
3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the office/service premises.
2) Move critical documents and supplies and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up client data, financial records and key contacts.
5) Test backup power (generator/UPS) and maintain an emergency fuel plan to keep essential equipment running.
Flood.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the office/service premises.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
5) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.

Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect critical documents and supplies: wrap palletized goods, raise critical stock, and cover machinery/equipment to prevent rainwater ingress.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.
Cyclone.Reference.Sources: NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Cyclones — https://nidm.gov.in/PDF/pubs/NDMA/4.pdf ; IMD – Cyclone Warning Services (overview) — https://mausam.imd.gov.in/imd_latest/contents/pdf/pubbrochures/Cyclone%20Warning%20Services.pdf ; BIS/Building Codes – Wind loads (IS 875 Part 3) reference — https://www.iitk.ac.in/nicee/IITK-GSDMA/W02.pdf ; ISO – ISO 22301 Business continuity management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/75106.html
Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the office/service premises.
2) Install and clearly label emergency shutoffs for electricity, gas and compressed air; ensure staff know how to operate them.
3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up client data, financial records and key contacts and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.
Earthquake.Reference.Sources: NDMA – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes — https://ndma.gov.in/sites/default/files/PDF/Guidelines/earthquakes.pdf ; NDMA – Simplified Guidelines for Earthquake Safety of Buildings — https://ndma.gov.in/sites/default/files/PDF/Guidelines/Simplified_Guidelines_for_earthquake.pdf ; BIS – Seismic design standards (e.g., IS 1893, IS 4326, IS 13920) — BIS Standards (refer latest editions) ; ISO – ISO 22301 Business continuity management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/75106.html
Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).
2) Before/after heavy rain, inspect and clear surface drains and culverts to prevent water buildup that can trigger slope failure.
3) Keep critical areas away from slope edges: avoid stacking heavy critical documents and supplies near retaining walls or steep embankments.
4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for access disruption: identify alternate routes/warehousing, and maintain contact lists for logistics, utilities and local authorities.
Landslide.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a geotechnical and slope-stability assessment; implement site-specific recommendations as a priority.
2) Improve slope drainage: lined drains, sub-surface drainage and proper runoff routing to reduce saturation of soil/rock.
3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

Drought.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize water for critical process and hygiene steps in the office/service premises; postpone non-critical cleaning/wash-downs where safe and permitted.
3) Introduce quick efficiency measures: low-flow nozzles, trigger hoses, dry-cleaning/sweeping before washing, and reuse of non-contact rinse water where appropriate.
4) Secure contingency supply: agreements for tanker/municipal supply and on-site storage; test water quality if used for food/health-related activities.
5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.

MSME.Description: Washing and (dry-) cleaning of textile and fur products
Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the office/service premises.
2) Move critical documents and supplies and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up client data, financial records and key contacts.
5) Test backup power (generator/UPS) and maintain an emergency fuel plan to keep essential equipment running.
Flood.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the office/service premises.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
5) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.
Flood.Reference.Sources: NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Floods — https://nidm.gov.in/pdf/guidelines/floods.pdf ; NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Urban Flooding — https://nidm.gov.in/pdf/guidelines/new/management_urban_flooding.pdf ; FEMA – P‑348 Protecting Building Utility Systems From Flood Damage — https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/fema_p-348_protecting_building_utility_systems_from_flood_damage_2017.pdf ; ISO – ISO 22301 Business continuity management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/75106.html
Drought.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize water for critical process and hygiene steps in the office/service premises; postpone non-critical cleaning/wash-downs where safe and permitted.
3) Introduce quick efficiency measures: low-flow nozzles, trigger hoses, dry-cleaning/sweeping before washing, and reuse of non-contact rinse water where appropriate.
4) Secure contingency supply: agreements for tanker/municipal supply and on-site storage; test water quality if used for food/health-related activities.
5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.
Drought.Reference.Sources: NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Drought — https://nidm.gov.in/PDF/pubs/NDMA/13.pdf ; CGWB – Rain Water Harvesting (Guide) — https://cgwb.gov.in/cgwbpnm/public/uploads/documents/1686136871443876411file.pdf ; ISO – ISO 46001 Water efficiency management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/68286.html ; ISO – ISO 22301 Business continuity management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/75106.html
Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect critical documents and supplies: wrap palletized goods, raise critical stock, and cover machinery/equipment to prevent rainwater ingress.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.
Cyclone.Reference.Sources: NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Cyclones — https://nidm.gov.in/PDF/pubs/NDMA/4.pdf ; IMD – Cyclone Warning Services (overview) — https://mausam.imd.gov.in/imd_latest/contents/pdf/pubbrochures/Cyclone%20Warning%20Services.pdf ; BIS/Building Codes – Wind loads (IS 875 Part 3) reference — https://www.iitk.ac.in/nicee/IITK-GSDMA/W02.pdf ; ISO – ISO 22301 Business continuity management systems — https://www.iso.org/standard/75106.html
Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).
2) Before/after heavy rain, inspect and clear surface drains and culverts to prevent water buildup that can trigger slope failure.
3) Keep critical areas away from slope edges: avoid stacking heavy critical documents and supplies near retaining walls or steep embankments.
4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for access disruption: identify alternate routes/warehousing, and maintain contact lists for logistics, utilities and local authorities.
Landslide.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a geotechnical and slope-stability assessment; implement site-specific recommendations as a priority.
2) Improve slope drainage: lined drains, sub-surface drainage and proper runoff routing to reduce saturation of soil/rock.
3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the office/service premises.
2) Install and clearly label emergency shutoffs for electricity, gas and compressed air; ensure staff know how to operate them.
3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up client data, financial records and key contacts and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.

Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.

4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.

Cyclone.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Monitor IMD cyclone bulletins and define clear trigger points for securing the site and suspending operations.
2) Secure the premises: brace/lock doors and windows, protect glazing, and move loose outdoor items and signage to prevent wind-borne damage.
3) Protect critical documents and supplies: wrap palletized goods, raise critical stock, and cover machinery/equipment to prevent rainwater ingress.
4) Prepare for power and communication loss: test backup generator/UPS, charge devices, and back up critical data to the cloud/off-site.
5) Make a people-safety plan: communicate evacuation/shelter procedures, keep emergency kits, and ensure safe shutdown of utilities.
Cyclone.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Strengthen wind resistance: retrofit roofs (tie-downs, bracing), install storm shutters/impact-resistant glazing, and secure rooftop equipment.
2) Ensure design/retrofit aligns with relevant building codes for wind loads and anchorage (especially for sheds, warehouses and signage).
3) Improve site drainage and stormwater management to prevent secondary flooding during cyclonic rainfall.
4) Create redundancy for critical utilities: backup power capacity, protected cabling, and alternate telecom links for operations and payments.
5) Formalize a cyclone business continuity plan: supplier alternatives, pre-negotiated repair contracts, and insurance coverage reviewed annually.
Cyclone.Reference.Sources: NDMA/NIDM – National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Cyclones — https://nidm.gov.in/PDF/pubs/NDMA/4.pdf ; IMD – Cyclone Warning Services (overview) — https://mausam.imd.gov.in/imd_latest/contents/pdf/pubbrochures/Cyclone%20Warning%20Services.pdf ; BIS/Building Codes – Wind loads (IS 875 Part 3) reference — https://www.iitk.ac.in/nicee/IITK-GSDMA/W02.pdf
Earthquake.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Secure non-structural hazards: anchor shelving/racking, restrain tall equipment, and store heavy items on lower levels in the office/service premises.
2) Install and clearly label emergency shutoffs for electricity, gas and compressed air; ensure staff know how to operate them.
3) Protect hazardous items: secure cylinders/chemicals, install spill containment, and keep pathways clear for evacuation.
4) Conduct simple drills and training: ‘Drop–Cover–Hold’ awareness, muster points, and a post-event inspection checklist.
5) Back up client data, financial records and key contacts and keep critical documents in waterproof/fire-safe storage; maintain emergency contact lists.
Earthquake.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a seismic vulnerability assessment of the building and retrofit where needed (strengthening columns, connections and bracing).
2) Anchor critical machinery and utilities: bolt down equipment, add flexible connections for pipes/ducts, and secure overhead services.
3) Upgrade critical lifelines: automatic gas shutoff valves, fire protection systems, and secure storage for hazardous substances.
4) Improve layout and storage practices: seismic-rated racking, restraints for cylinders, and safe clearances around exits and emergency routes.
5) Implement a formal business continuity and recovery plan, including alternate operating location and rapid repair contractors.

Heatwave.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Adopt a simple Heat Action Plan: monitor heat alerts, designate a supervisor, and define work-rest and hydration breaks.
2) Reduce heat exposure: shift heavy work to cooler hours, increase ventilation, provide shaded rest areas and cool drinking water.
3) Protect heat-sensitive critical documents and supplies and equipment: verify cooling setpoints, service HVAC/chillers, and keep critical spares for cooling systems.
4) Train staff to recognize heat illness and respond quickly; maintain a first-aid protocol and emergency contact arrangements.
5) Reduce indoor heat gain: close blinds during peak sun, use fans/air movement safely, and limit use of heat-generating equipment in peak hours.
6) For outdoor workers: enforce buddy system, provide electrolyte solutions, and stop work if symptoms appear or heat index crosses thresholds.
Heatwave.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Improve building thermal performance: cool roofs (reflective coatings), insulation, shading and natural ventilation design.
2) Upgrade to energy-efficient cooling systems sized for peak heat; consider zoned cooling for critical areas to reduce costs.
3) Install temperature monitoring and alarms (cold rooms, server rooms, critical production spaces) with preventive maintenance schedules.
4) Create longer-term workforce adaptations: heat-safe uniforms/PPE, annual training before summer, and paid rest breaks during severe heat alerts.
5) Reduce dependency on grid power: solar + battery/backup solutions to keep essential cooling and IT running during peak demand outages.
Heatwave.Reference.Sources: NDMA/NIDM – Prevention and Management of Heat Wave (Guidelines) — https://nidm.gov.in/PDF/pubs/NDMA/27.pdf ; NDMA – Beating the Heat (IEC booklet) — https://ndma.gov.in/sites/default/files/IEC/Booklets/HeatWave%20A5%20BOOK%20Final.pdf ; WHO – Climate change and workplace heat stress (guidance) — https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099814
Landslide.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Check if the site or approach roads are in a landslide-prone zone; monitor visible warning signs (new cracks, tilting poles, blocked drains).
2) Before/after heavy rain, inspect and clear surface drains and culverts to prevent water buildup that can trigger slope failure.
3) Keep critical areas away from slope edges: avoid stacking heavy critical documents and supplies near retaining walls or steep embankments.
4) Set a rainfall-trigger protocol: pause operations and restrict access during intense rainfall; define evacuation routes and muster points.
5) Plan continuity for access disruption: identify alternate routes/warehousing, and maintain contact lists for logistics, utilities and local authorities.
Landslide.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Commission a geotechnical and slope-stability assessment; implement site-specific recommendations as a priority.
2) Improve slope drainage: lined drains, sub-surface drainage and proper runoff routing to reduce saturation of soil/rock.
3) Stabilize slopes where needed: retaining structures, soil nailing/rock bolting, gabions and bio-engineering/vegetation with expert design.
4) Reduce exposure: relocate critical storage/operations away from unstable slopes; avoid new construction in high-susceptibility zones.
5) Create a monitoring and maintenance plan (inspections, instrumentation where feasible) and review insurance/BCP for prolonged access outages.

MSME.Description: Mining and quarrying
Flood.Short-term.Resilience.Actions:
1) Set up a flood readiness checklist: monitor local alerts, assign roles, and mark shut‑off points for electricity/gas/water in the office/service premises.
2) Move critical documents and supplies and critical spares to higher racks/floors (or off‑site storage) before water enters; protect items in waterproof crates where possible.
3) Reduce water ingress: install temporary flood boards/sandbags at entrances, seal low-level vents, and clear drains/gutters around the site.
4) Protect utilities and IT: cover or switch off vulnerable electrical panels, move servers/POS terminals to higher levels, and back up client data, financial records and key contacts.
5) Test backup power (generator/UPS) and maintain an emergency fuel plan to keep essential equipment running.
Flood.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Conduct a site-specific flood risk assessment (including historical flooding and drainage) and define trigger levels for planned shutdown/restart.
2) Invest in permanent flood protection: flood‑resistant doors/barriers, raised thresholds, and waterproofing for ground‑floor areas of the office/service premises.
3) Floodproof critical utilities: elevate electrical panels, generators, compressors and pumps; use water‑resistant conduits and quick‑disconnects for faster recovery.
4) Upgrade drainage and backflow control: install non‑return valves, sumps/pumps with redundancy, and preventive maintenance contracts before monsoon season.
5) Strengthen continuity arrangements: alternative storage/production options, supplier diversification, and adequate insurance coverage supported by an updated asset register.

1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize water for critical process and hygiene steps in the office/service premises; postpone non-critical cleaning/wash-downs where safe and permitted.
3) Introduce quick efficiency measures: low-flow nozzles, trigger hoses, dry-cleaning/sweeping before washing, and reuse of non-contact rinse water where appropriate.
4) Secure contingency supply: agreements for tanker/municipal supply and on-site storage; test water quality if used for food/health-related activities.
5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.

1) Track daily water use and fix visible leaks immediately; set a minimum-water operating mode for non-essential activities.
2) Prioritize water for critical process and hygiene steps in the plants/substations and distribution infrastructure; postpone non-critical cleaning/wash-downs where safe and permitted.
3) Introduce quick efficiency measures: low-flow nozzles, trigger hoses, dry-cleaning/sweeping before washing, and reuse of non-contact rinse water where appropriate.
4) Secure contingency supply: agreements for tanker/municipal supply and on-site storage; test water quality if used for food/health-related activities.
5) Update production/service schedules to avoid water-intensive peaks and communicate conservation SOPs to all staff.
Drought.Long-term.Resilience.Measures:
1) Install rainwater harvesting and/or recharge structures sized to roof and site area, with first-flush diversion and routine cleaning.
2) Upgrade to water-efficient fixtures and process equipment (closed-loop cooling, low-flow taps, optimized cleaning-in-place).
3) Invest in water recycling: ETP/STP upgrades and safe reuse in non-potable applications (gardening, flushing, cooling towers).
4) Build supplier resilience: diversify water-intensive inputs and maintain buffer stocks for critical consumables during restrictions.
5) Adopt a documented water efficiency management plan with targets, monitoring, periodic audits and staff training.
